title: Multispectral Optoacoustic Imaging (MSOT) to Investigate Cerebrovascular Disease
off: Multispectral Optoacoustic Imaging (MSOT) to Investigate Cerebrovascular Disease: A Single Center, Observational Study Using the MSOT Acuity in Cerebrovascular Disease

officials.a: University hospital of Zurich, Department of Neurology

summary:
Stenosis of the internal carotid artery (ICA) is a common cause of ischemic stroke. Current clinical guidelines focus primarily on the degree of stenosis to determine treatment strategies, such as medical management, endovascular stenting, or surgical endarterectomy. However, the morphology and tissue composition of plaques are increasingly recognized as critical factors for stroke risk, as even mild-to-moderate stenosis may harbor dangerous, vulnerable plaques at risk of rupture. Conventional imaging modalities, such as duplex sonography, provide limited information regarding specific plaque characteristics and vessel wall inflammation, making the discrimination between atherosclerotic and inflammatory diseases a persistent diagnostic challenge. This study utilizes multi-spectral optoacoustic tomography (MSOT), a non-invasive imaging approach that combines ultrasound with laser technology to visualize disease-specific tissue biomarkers. MSOT offers the advantage of assessing specific tissue components, including lipid content, water, collagen, and oxygenation status (oxy- and deoxyhemoglobin), which serve as key indicators of plaque instability, vascularization, and inflammation.

The primary goal of this project is to evaluate the clinical utility of MSOT biomarker signals in characterising carotid plaques and inflammatory vessel wall changes. Investigators aim to find a definitive relation between these tissue-specific MSOT signals within the carotid artery, carotid plaques, and the superficial temporal artery, and relate them to the type (atherosclerosis versus inflammation) and severity of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease. The study encompasses both patients with manifest cardiovascular disease and healthy subjects with cardiovascular risk factors to explore applications in both advanced disease characterization and primary prevention.
desc:
Stenosis of the internal carotid artery (ICA) is a common cause of ischemic stroke. Treatment guidelines were established in the 1990s from the results of the large North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET) and the European Carotid Surgery Trial (ECST). Current recommendations for the management of ICA stenosis focus on stenosis degree and include medical treatment, endovascular carotid artery stenting, as well as surgical carotid endarterectomy. Briefly, if stenosis degree approaches 70%, surgical or endovascular treatment may be indicated. However, over the last 30 years, standard medical care has dramatically improved, and decision-making in cases of ICA stenosis is becoming more complex. The relevance of morphology and composition of plaques for stroke risk in ICA stenosis patients is increasingly recognized. Accordingly, even a stenosis degree of 40% or 50% may harbor a dangerous plaque at risk of rupture.

Duplex sonography is a state-of-the-art imaging modality used to assess ICA stenosis in patients with stroke or patients at risk of stroke. Although it is a very powerful and versatile method, it can only extract few characteristics of the plaque and the associated vessel wall. Furthermore, inflammatory changes of the vessel wall are difficult to assess with duplex sonography or other imaging methods such as Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). Such inflammation is involved in atherosclerotic plaque development and may indicate a vulnerable plaque. At the same time, inflammation of the vessel wall is pathognomonic for vasculitis of the nervous system. The discrimination of atherosclerotic from inflammatory disease remains a challenge in stroke diagnosis and treatment.

The goal of the current project is to characterize ICA plaques or inflammatory vessel wall changes in patients with cardiovascular disease and healthy subjects with cardiovascular risk factors. Multispectral Optoacoustic Tomography (MSOT) is a non-invasive approach for carotid plaque visualization and characterization. MSOT has the unique advantage of imaging disease-specific biomarkers in addition to conventional ultrasound methods. For carotid imaging, specific assessment of lipid content and oxygenation state are particularly interesting, since lipid accumulation and plaque vascularization are key indicators of plaque formation and advancement towards instability and stroke risk.

The investigators aim at: 1) characterizing the vulnerable carotid plaque, 2) differentiating atherosclerotic from inflammatory vessel wall changes, and 3) characterizing subclinical pathology (lipid accumulation, inflammation) in the vessel wall of patients with vascular risk factors, but without stroke (primary prevention). The MSOT Acuity is a CE-certified device to detect and visualize photo-absorbers in soft tissue.

The hypothesis is that lipid, water, oxy-/deoxyhemoglobin content, and collagen signals strongly relate to the type (atherosclerosis versus inflammation) and severity of cerebrovascular disease. The primary objective is to find a relation of the new MSOT biomarker signals (lipid, water, oxy-/deoxyhemoglobin, and collagen content) of the carotid artery/plaque and the superficial temporal artery (STA) to the type (atherosclerosis versus inflammation) and severity of cardiovascular disease.
elig:
Inclusion Criteria:

* 18 years or older
* written informed consent
* patient with carotid artery plaques (detected by ultrasound) either hospitalized because of ischemic symptoms or asymptomatic (ambulatory).
* patients with suspicion of giant cell arteritis (from clinical or ophthalmological diagnosis) either hospitalized because of symptoms or ambulatory, regardless of treatment with steroids
* healthy subjects

Exclusion Criteria:

* pregnant patients
* Participants unable to tolerate MSOT measurements (approx. 15min with laser protection goggles)
* Patients not available for at least first follow up after 3 months, or with severe comorbidity likely to interfere with a follow up at 3 months
* Tattoos, hypersensitivity, Skin lesions or Fitzpatrick skin type I, V and VI at the site of MSOT investigation

arms.d: Healthy subjects without plaques in the extra cranial carotid arteries who haven't suffered from stroke yet.

Patients with plaques in the extra cranial carotid arteries,, who have suffered from stroke before enrollment
Patients who have been diagnosed with or suspected of suffering from giant cell arteritis in the superficial temporal arteries before enrollment.
